[72]   There is no reason to conclude that the justice of the peace intended to make a mandatory order banning publication of information that might identify a witness over the age of 17 years in this case. There was no request for such an order. There is no evidence that any such witness was involved in the case at the time the request was made. Ms. M. was not at the bail hearing and had never discussed the publication ban with the Crown before testifying at the sentencing hearing. Indeed, she did not even know she was going to be asked to take the witness stand at the sentencing hearing until she was called upon to do so.

[73]   Thus, there is no evidence that the court intended to make an order that it could not make under s. 486.4 and, therefore, there is no need to quash the order.

Section 442(3) is one of the measures adopted by Parliament to remedy this situation, the rationale being that a victim who fears publicity is assured, when deciding whether to report the crime or not, that the judge must prohibit upon request the publication of the complainant's identity or any information that could disclose it.  Obviously, since fear of publication is one one of the factors that influences the reporting of sexual assault, certainty with respect to non-publication at the time of deciding whether to report plays a vital role in that decision.  Therefore, a discretionary provision under which the judge retains the power to decide whether to grant or refuse the ban on publication would be counterproductive, since it would deprive the victim of that certainty.

facts.text: The judge may issue a publication ban to protect the identity of a victim or witness in cases involving specific sexual or violent offences, including those related to domestic violence.
facts.why_it_matters: This is the core legal requirement under s. 486.4 of the Criminal Code, which allows for the protection of identities in certain cases. The specific list of offences includes many that could be relevant to domestic violence.
facts.if_changed: If the case does not involve one of the listed offences, the judge may not have the authority to issue a publication ban.

facts.text: A publication ban is mandatory if requested by the prosecutor, but only for victims or witnesses under the age of 18.
facts.why_it_matters: Under s. 486.4(2)(b), the prosecutor can request a mandatory publication ban on behalf of a victim or witness under 18. This is a key distinction from those over 18, who may still be protected but not mandatorily.
facts.if_changed: If the witness or victim is over 18, the judge has discretion, and the protection is not automatic.

facts.text: The judge must inquire whether the victim or witness wishes to be protected by the order, especially if they are present in court.
facts.why_it_matters: This is a procedural requirement under s. 486.4(3.1), ensuring that the victim or witness is aware of and consents to the protection order.
facts.if_changed: If the judge fails to inquire, the order may be invalid or subject to challenge.

facts.text: The court must balance the right to a fair trial and public access to court proceedings against the need to protect the victim or witness from harm.
facts.why_it_matters: Under s. 486.5(7), the court must consider factors such as the risk of harm, the effectiveness of alternatives, and the impact on freedom of expression.
facts.if_changed: If the court does not properly balance these factors, the order may be deemed disproportionate or unjustified.

facts.text: The protection order does not apply if the disclosure is made in the course of the administration of justice for non-public purposes.
facts.why_it_matters: This is a key limitation under s. 486.4(4)(a), which allows for exceptions when the disclosure is necessary for the legal process and not for public dissemination.
facts.if_changed: If the disclosure is made for public purposes, the protection order would still apply.

facts.text: The victim or witness has the right to apply to revoke or vary the order, and the prosecutor must inform them of this right.
facts.why_it_matters: Under s. 486.4(3.2), the prosecutor is required to inform the victim or witness of their right to seek changes to the order.
facts.if_changed: If the victim or witness is not informed, the order may be challenged on procedural grounds.

facts.text: The court must consider whether there are less restrictive alternatives to protect the identity of the victim or witness.
facts.why_it_matters: Under s. 486.5(7)(e), the court must determine if other measures could achieve the same protection without limiting public access to the courts.
facts.if_changed: If less restrictive alternatives exist, the court may be required to use them instead of a full publication ban.

facts.text: The protection order does not apply to disclosures made by the victim or witness themselves, provided the purpose is not to make the information public.
facts.why_it_matters: Under s. 486.4(5), the victim or witness can disclose their own identity without violating the order, as long as it is not for public dissemination.
facts.if_changed: If the victim or witness discloses their identity publicly, they may be in violation of the order.
